sections.html:
Three roles, three places: the Trustee collects, the Assessor values, and the County Commission votes on the rate. The first two are neighbors on Public Square in Columbia, and each is open weekdays from eight until four.

  • Trustee: One Public Square, Columbia, TN 38401, 931-375-2201. Make checks out to Maury County Trustee and mail them to that address.
  • Assessor of Property: 6 Public Square, Columbia, TN 38401, 931-375-4001.
  • Rate: voted each year by the Maury County Commission.

The person who held title on New Year's Day gets the bill, and new mailing addresses go to the Assessor, as the Trustee's page explains. Living in Columbia, Spring Hill or Mount Pleasant? Check with that city's hall for a separate city bill.

Maury County lies south of Nashville and has grown fast. Columbia holds the courthouse, and Spring Hill, which straddles the Williamson County line, is the largest city. The county counted 118,131 people on July 1, 2025, up 17.0% from April 2020, and has 49,725 housing units, 70.9% of them owner-occupied. A typical owner-occupied house is valued at $355,700, typical rent is $1,300, and the median household earns $76,130. Builders pulled 1,408 permits in 2025.

Interstate 65, State Route 396 and US 31 tie the county to Nashville, which explains much of the demand. Maury County Public Schools runs the public schools countywide. For a seller, fast growth means buyers are comparing many new listings, so a clean tax record and an accurate assessment help your house hold its own.

Maury County values every property afresh on a four-year rhythm, and this is one of those years. The figure on file reflects what the market was paying on January 1, 2026, with later improvements layered on at equalized value. Because prices have risen a lot, anyone whose house was last valued before that run-up should study the new notice.

The arithmetic is brief: appraised value times the ratio for the property class, then the rate applied to every $100 of that. Houses are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value statewide.

The county's 2025 to 2026 budget letter to the state Comptroller shows a rate of $1.91 for each $100 of assessment, with no increase for residents. A reappraisal year can bring a different rate, so ask the Trustee which one is on your current bill. The Assessor's page explains the calculation and links to reappraisal guides.

You can start paying in early October and have until the end of February, and bills are due as soon as you receive them. Starting March 1, penalty and interest of 1.5 percent accrue and keep growing monthly. On April 1, any account still open is sent to Chancery Court.

Part payments are fine with the Trustee, but whatever is unpaid on March 1 starts earning interest. The postmark date counts as your payment date, apart from accounts already moved to Chancery Court. A county is not required to mail notices under Tennessee law, so you cannot dodge the charges by pointing to a bill that never came.

  • In person at One Public Square, or in the drop box outside the office (no cash)
  • By mail to Maury County Trustee, One Public Square, Columbia, TN 38401
  • Online by credit card or e-check, with a 2.5% vendor fee
  • By phone at 1-877-556-4502
  • Monthly bank debits through the county's ACH program, set up by calling 931-375-2201

sections.h2: How to contest a new value
sections.html:
Climb three steps in order: the Assessor, the county equalization board, then the state board. For this year's county board process, call 931-375-4001.

The later steps are laid out in the state's appeals guide. Skip the county board and the value usually becomes final. Your state deadline is August 1 or the 45th day after the county board mailed notice, whichever comes later, so count from the mailing date if your county notice was late. After the hearing an administrative judge has 90 days to rule, and a court petition must be filed within 60 days of the state order becoming final.

An informal review, where an assessor offers one, can speed up a fix, yet it is not an appeal and preserves no rights. Ask whether Maury's office does one, and file with the county board regardless.

Before you call the Assessor, write down your parcel number, the value on the notice, and why you think it is off. Pull sales of similar houses nearby, note any differences in size, age and condition, and keep photos of problems such as a worn roof or foundation cracks. Specific evidence makes the conversation shorter and gives the county board something concrete to weigh.

The Trustee's office helps elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled-veteran owners and the widows or widowers of a disabled veteran apply for the Tennessee Tax Relief Program under state guidelines. Call 931-375-2201 for the forms and the current income limits.

Through the ACH program, the bill can be split into equal monthly bank debits; call that number to enroll. Splitting it avoids one large payment in February, though every debit has to clear before March 1 charges begin.

Tax years match calendar years, and the January 1 owner receives the notice. After a fall sale the seller's name stays on the bill, although the buyer takes the house into the next year. Ask the Trustee for the exact balance and have the title agent divide it at closing.

A seller who lists late has little time, since charges begin in March and Chancery Court follows in April. Whatever is open at closing is deducted from your net proceeds. Confirm the figure with the Trustee about a week before.

Gather four things before you list: the latest bill, proof of any monthly debits, relief paperwork, and the Assessor's value notice. A house held by a family for years deserves a look at older years too, since a balance may be hiding there. Cash buyers can close quickly, and the Trustee's payoff is still paid at the table. Keep copies of every receipt, because the title agent may ask for proof that a payment cleared. If a bill is already late, call the Trustee at 931-375-2201 for a current figure rather than relying on an old statement, since interest grows every month.

faqs.q: Is 2026 a reappraisal year in Maury County?
faqs.a: Yes. A new appraisal comes every four years, and the current one is 2026, based on market prices as of January 1.

faqs.q: What rate does Maury County use?
faqs.a: The 2025 to 2026 budget letter lists $1.91 per $100 of assessed value. Since the Commission sets it, confirm the figure on your bill or with the Trustee.

faqs.q: When do Maury County taxes become late?
faqs.a: March 1 is when charges of 1.5 percent a month begin, and April 1 is when delinquent accounts go to Chancery Court. You can pay from the first Monday in October through February.

faqs.q: Does Maury County accept partial payments?
faqs.a: Yes. Any balance left on March 1 still accrues interest, so a part payment shrinks the amount earning interest without stopping it.

faqs.q: Where do I send a new mailing address?
faqs.a: Tell the Assessor, at 931-375-4001. The Trustee sends address changes there, and a missing bill does not cancel penalty or interest.
